q: In the output of 'ss -tulpn' you see 0.0.0.0:6379 (Redis). What does that mean?
options: Redis listens on all interfaces and is reachable by anyone who can reach the server over the network
explain: 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 interfaces. A service used only by local applications should bind to 127.0.0.1, or at least have a firewall/security group restricting access.

q: nmap shows a port as 'filtered'. What is most likely?
options: The service is running and accepting connections
The host replied with RST, nothing is listening
No response: the packet was probably dropped by a firewall
explain: open = something is listening, closed = the host replied with RST, filtered = no response or an ICMP 'unreachable', typically due to a firewall.

q: What does forward secrecy in TLS protect?
options: Previously captured traffic stays protected even if the server's private key leaks later
It prevents MITM without a certificate
explain: With (EC)DHE, session keys are ephemeral and not derived from the server's long-term key, so stealing that key doesn't unlock past sessions.

q: curl reports 'unable to get local issuer certificate', but the browser opens the site without errors. Most common cause?
options: The server doesn't send the intermediate certificate in the chain
explain: Browsers often fill in a missing intermediate on their own (cache, AIA fetching), while curl and application libraries don't. The server should send the full chain, excluding the root.

q: What does a client use to verify that a certificate belongs to the host it is connecting to?
explain: Modern clients compare the hostname against the SAN field. Relying on CN is deprecated and browsers ignore it.

q: Which TLS versions are acceptable under current recommendations (Mozilla intermediate, NIST)? (multiple answers)
explain: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated (RFC 8996), and SSL was broken long ago. Today TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are used.

q: What is the core idea of the zero trust model?
options: Trust no one, so block all traffic
Network location doesn't grant trust; every request is verified based on identity, device and context
Replace the firewall with a VPN
explain: Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207) doesn't mean 'block everything', but that trust is not derived from someone being 'inside'. Verification is continuous and per request.

q: Why is controlling OUTBOUND (egress) traffic important?
options: Malware has to communicate with a C2 server and exfiltrate data, and restricted egress makes that harder and more visible
It doesn't matter if ingress is protected
explain: If a database server may not open connections to the internet, a compromise has a harder time turning into exfiltration and C2. Unexpected outbound traffic is also a good detection signal.

q: What is the best starting mode when introducing a WAF in front of an existing application?
options: Block mode for all rules right away
Detection/count mode, analyze false positives, then gradually block
WAF only in the staging environment
explain: Going straight to block easily breaks legitimate requests. Observe first, tune exceptions, then block.

q: Which sign in DNS logs points to DNS tunneling?
options: Many queries with long, random subdomains to a single domain
explain: Tunneling encodes data in subdomain names, so you see long, high-entropy names and an unusually high number of queries to the same domain.

q: In Kubernetes a pod has no NetworkPolicy at all. What traffic is allowed?
explain: By default everything is allowed. Only once a policy 'selects' a pod does deny apply to it, except for what the policies allow. That's why a default-deny policy per namespace is good practice.

q: This nginx configuration should match the Mozilla "intermediate" profile from the lesson. Click the line that violates it.
explain: ssl_protocols includes TLSv1 and TLSv1.1, which are obsolete and disabled in the intermediate profile. The correct line is ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;. The ciphers are ECDHE with AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), so they provide forward secrecy, HSTS is set, and proxy_pass to localhost is normal TLS termination on the same host.
